newsitem.title: INDIA: India analysts differ on ITC scandal impact.
newsitem.headline: India analysts differ on ITC scandal impact.

text.p: Priya Ramani
Stock analysts were divided on Monday on whether investors in India's biggest cigarette company, ITC Ltd, should sell or hold on to their shares in the firm enmeshed in a foreign exchange scandal.
Some analysts advised investors to bail out while others cited the Indian tobacco firm's core strengths as reasons to hold the stock.
ITC shares have plunged 10 percent on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) in less than a week, pounded by news of the scandal.
Last week, the nation's Enforcement Directorate searched the firm's offices and arrested senior officials including two former chairmen.
The directorate, the watchdog over issues related to corporate finances, is investigating alleged violations of foreign exchange rules by the cigarette maker.
The Finance Ministry said in a statement last week that evidence indicated "violations by ITC Ltd to the tune of over $100 million".
ITC shares were trading at 288.50 rupees on Monday in afternoon trade, 10.5 rupees lower than Friday's close.

"The enormity and scale of this development, coupled with the fact that many senior management personnel may be involved, tremendously increases the risk profile of the company," analyst Rukhshad Shroff at Jardine Fleming India Broking said in a report.
Shroff said given that the stock had increased 22 percent since a "buy" recommendation issued in September 1995, investors should "sell and take profits."

An analyst at a European brokerage firm said in a note to investors that Britain's tobacco and financial group, B.A.T Industries Plc -- which controls 31.7 percent of ITC -- could come to the rescue with an infusion of funds and a change in management.

"However, we believe that the worst for the company is not yet over... We believe in the short- to medium-term, there is a great deal of uncertainty regarding the company's day-to-day running and growth prospects," she warned, advising investors to avoid the stock.
Broking firms Peregrine Capital and UBS Securities reiterated sell recommendations in notes to their investors.
"The risks in the stock have still to crystallise," said UBS analyst Sandeep Bhatia.
Peregrine analyst Thygesh Baba said although changes in senior management were inevitable, they would take time to materialise.
"Top level decision-making is most likely to come to a standstill...In the process, ITC could end up losing 3.0 percent to 4.0 percent market share to competition in the medium term," he said.
But others said attractive valuations prevented them from downgrading the stock.

"The projected earnings growth for 1996/97 (April-March) is 52.8 percent driven by improved operating margin on the back of larger volumes... We feel this is an attractive valuation for a company in the consumer sector with a dominant and growing market share," analyst K. Ramachandran at Birla Marlin Securities said in a report.
Ramachandran said the scandal would hit ITC's image but would not seriously impact finances. He advised a "strong buy".
Sujay Mishra, analyst at securities firm SSKI said investors should pick up the stock at 250 rupee-levels.
"There will be a big rerating of the stock if B.A.T comes into the picture. Besides, the fundamentals remain good. One should not panic and sell," he said.
